hook: In a meadow, energy from the sun passes from grass to a grasshopper to a frog to a snake to a hawk. Each step is a trophic level, a rung on the ladder of who eats whom. Knowing an organism’s level tells you where its energy comes from and what happens to it when the level below shrinks.

options: An organism that makes its own food from light
One organism kills and eats another
One species lives on another without harming it

figure.caption: Trophic levels in a meadow, from producers to an apex predator.

chain.cause: Secondary and tertiary consumers eat the level below
chain.effect: they form levels 3 and 4, up to an apex predator

ideas: A trophic level is an organism’s position in the feeding sequence: producers are 1, primary consumers 2, secondary 3, tertiary 4.
Herbivores eat producers; carnivores eat animals; omnivores eat both and feed at more than one level.
An apex predator is at the top with no natural predators as an adult.
Arrows point from food to eater, the direction energy moves.

misconception.wrong: Arrows in a food diagram point from the predator to what it eats.
misconception.right: Arrows show where the energy goes: from the food to the eater. Grass → grasshopper means the grasshopper eats the grass.

summary: Trophic levels sort organisms by how they get energy. Producers (level 1) make food from light; primary consumers (herbivores, level 2) eat producers; secondary and tertiary consumers eat the levels below; an apex predator is at the top. Omnivores feed at more than one level. Arrows point from food to eater, so a change at one level ripples to the others.
